ATLANTIC SKIES: Could the Milky Way's Sagittarius A* be something other than a black hole?

It's long been theorized that the Milky Way's Sagittarius A* is a black hole, but a new theory suggests an alternate model

Last updated 5 hours ago

It has long been theorized that a supermassive black hole lies at the very centre of our Milky Way Galaxy.

Referred to as the Sagittarius A star (Sag A*), this huge, unseen object is estimated to have a mass of approximately 4.3 million solar masses (one solar mass equals the mass of our sun), and is located around 27,000 light-years (one light-year equals approximately 9,460,730,472,580.8 kilometres) from Earth in the constellation of Sagittarius – the Archer.

It cannot be directly observed due to the fact that it is shrouded by dense clouds of interstellar dust.

Black holes were first theorized by American physicist and radio engineer Karl Jansky (1905-1950) after he detected an unusual radio signal emanating from the direction of the Sagittarius constellation in April 1933.

Numerous theories arose as to what this signal represented, ranging from clouds of star clusters to a supernova remnant. By the 1950s, however, it was generally accepted by most astrophysicists that whatever the object was, it was associated with the centre of the Milky Way Galaxy.

Then, in February 1974, astronomers Bruce Balik and Robert L. Brown in Green Bank, West Virginia, USA, identified the object as a single, compact body. It was Brown who, due to the object’s perceived location within the Sagittarius constellation (as viewed from Earth), named it Sagittarius A star (Sag A*).

Black holes are theoretical (i.e., have not been definitively proven) astronomical bodies so dense that their gravity prevents anything, even light, from escaping. It was the German-born theoretical physicist Albert Einstein (1879-1955) who, in his 1916 general theory of relativity, first described gravity as the curvature of spacetime, and who proposed that any sufficiently compact mass will form a black hole.

In the 1990s, astronomers were able to observe numerous stars, referred to as ‘S stars’, orbiting an apparently empty region of space in the location of Sag A*.

These stars, the closest known stars to Sag A*, were travelling at tremendous speeds, up to 24,000 km/sec or in excess of 86 million km /hr (approximately eight per cent the speed of light). These stars were obviously being influenced by an object millions of times more massive than our sun.

By tracking the orbital motion of these stars, astronomers were able to calculate the size of Sag A* at roughly 23.5-25 million kilometres across, slightly smaller than the orbit of Venus around the sun.

These calculations ultimately led to three astronomers — Roger Penrose (University of Oxford, UK), for his discovery that black hole formation is a robust prediction of Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity; Reinhard Genzel (Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, Germany) and Andrea Ghez (University of California, Los Angeles, USA) — being awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020.

The theory that Sag A* is a supermassive black hole was given a strong boost when the now-famous photograph of Sag A* was released in 2022.

Taken by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), a global network of radio telescopes, the photo purported to show a black globe-like body surrounded by swirling streaks of light.

The photo aligned with what a black hole was theorized to look like, with the only light visible being generated as matter in the vicinity of the black hole was super-heated as it spun around the circumference of the black hole, which, itself would not be visible due to the fact that nothing, not even light, escapes once it has crossed the black hole’s event horizon and disappears into the black hole.

However, although the EHT photo shows what is believed to be a black hole, and although the general consensus in the global astronomical community is that Sag A* is most likely a supermassive black hole, it has not been definitively proven.

In fact, the wording of the 2020 Nobel Physics Award specifically states that it was “for the discovery of a supermassive compact object at the center of our galaxy” — not for the discovery of a black hole. As such, this wording’s ambiguity leaves open the door for alternate theories to be proposed as to what Sag A* is.

In February 2026, Valentina Crespi at the Institute of Astrophysics La Plata in Buenos Aires, Argentina, who studies dark matter at galactic scales, proposed an alternate black hole model.

Based on her theory that Sag A* is composed of a dense dark matter core, Crespi and her colleagues statistically compared the observational data of the S2 stars, along with five known ‘G objects’ — a unique class of objects thought to be dense, compact clouds of dust, that, although behaving like actual stars, resemble clouds of gas, altering their shape the closer they get to Sag A*’s due to its intense gravity.

Crespi sought to determine whether or not a large dark matter core could influence the behaviour of the S stars and G objects orbiting Sag A* to the same degree of precision as demonstrated in the black hole model.

Her conclusions, published in the February 2026 issue of the Journal of Royal Astronomical Society, suggested that a large, dense core of dark matter with sufficient mass could, in fact, reproduce the orbits of the S stars and G objects with less than one per cent difference to the black hole model, signifying an inability to distinguish between a dark matter core and a black hole, given the observational data currently available.

It should be understood, however, as Crespi and her team were quick to point out, that this new, radical dark matter core theory for Sag A* has not been proven and, as a consequence, does not disprove the theory that Sag A* is a supermassive black hole.

No doubt, it will take a great deal more research into the nature and properties of Sag A* to determine exactly what sort of astronomical entity it is.

In the meantime, science needs to keep an open mind; there is still much that is unknown about the universe, even at the very center of our own galaxy.

Mercury (mag. -0.3, in Virgo – the Maiden), now past its greatest elongation west of the sun, is visible in the dawn sky, rising around 5:35 a.m. AST and reaching 12 degrees above the southeast horizon before fading from view by about 7 a.m. AST.

Venus (mag. -4.6, in Virgo), now emerging into the morning sky as it nears its greatest elongation west of the sun, rises around 4:10 a.m. AST, reaching 25 degrees above the southeast horizon before fading from view shortly after 7 a.m. AST. On Nov. 27, Venus will be at its greatest brightness (mag. -4.7) of its 2026 -2027 morning apparition.

Mars (mag. +0.7, in Leo – the Lion), visible in the early morning sky, becomes accessible around 12:15 a.m. AST, 11 degrees above the eastern horizon, reaching its highest point in the sky 57 degrees above the southern horizon by about 6:10 a.m. AST, before being lost to the dawn twilight around 6:45 a.m. AST, 56 degrees above the southern horizon.

Jupiter (mag. -2.1, in Leo), currently emerging from behind the sun (superior solar conjunction), becomes accessible around 11:50 p.m. AST when it’s seven degrees above the eastern horizon, reaching its highest point in the sky 57 degrees above the southern horizon by about 6 a.m. AST, before getting lost in the dawn twilight 54 degrees above the southwest horizon around 7:05 a.m. AST.

Saturn (mag. +0.4, in Cetus – the Sea Monster), visible in the evening sky, becomes accessible 26 degrees above the southeast horizon by about 5:15 p.m. AST, reaching its highest point in the sky 44 degrees above the southern horizon around 8:35 p.m. AST, and remaining observable until around 1:35 a.m. AST, when it sinks below 10 degrees above the western horizon.

Uranus (mag. +5.6, in Taurus – the Bull), due to reach opposition on Nov. 25, becomes accessible 21 degrees above the eastern horizon by about 6:50 p.m. AST, reaching its highest point in the sky 64 degrees above the southern horizon around 12:10 a.m. AST, before becoming inaccessible by 5:30 a.m. AST, when it drops below 21 degrees above the western horizon.

Neptune (mag. +7.8, in Pisces – the Fish), visible in the evening sky, becomes accessible when it reaches 33 degrees above the southeast horizon by about 5:50 p.m. AST, reaching its highest point in the sky 43 degrees above the southern horizon around 8:10 p.m. AST, and remaining observable until around 11:55 p.m. AST, when it sinks below 21 degrees above the southwest horizon.

Visible between Nov. 13 and Dec. 6, the November Orionids meteor shower will peak during the overnight period of Nov. 27-28, with the best viewing coming closer to dawn.

The shower’s radiant (the apparent point of origin in the night sky as seen from Earth) lies at the base of the raised club of Orion – the Hunter, slightly north of the famous red supergiant star Betelgeuse in the upper left-hand corner of Orion’s torso. Orion will clear the eastern horizon around 6:30 p.m AST.

Although the parent body of the November Orionids remains uncertain, it is thought to possibly be associated with comet C/1917 F1 (Mellish), discovered by American amateur astronomer John E. Mellish (1886-1970) on March 19, 1917.

Unfortunately, this year the shower peaks a few days after the full moon on Nov. 24, so light from the bright, waning gibbous moon, which will be up most of the night, will wash out many of the meteors.

Under a dark sky away from city lights, between midnight and morning twilight, expect to see about three to five meteors per hour. However, as with all meteor showers, the number of meteors visible could vary considerably from year to year, with the possibility of many more seen per hour than predicted.

The full moon on Nov. 24 is sometimes still referred to as the “Beaver Moon,” as the late fall season is the time of year when beavers typically begin to take shelter in their lodges in preparation for the approaching winter season. As well, historically, it is also the time of year when beavers were hunted for their thick, winter-ready pelts.

Until next week, clear skies.

Events:
Nov. 24 – Full “Beaver Moon” at 10:53 a.m. AST
Nov. 25 – Moon at perigee (closest approach to Earth) at 5:01 p.m. AST (356,500 km); Uranus at opposition at 6:33 p.m. AST
Nov. 27 – Venus at greatest brightness of 2026-2027 morning apparition.
Nov. 28 – November Orionid meteor shower peaks; close approach (appulse) of moon and M44 (Beehive Cluster in Cancer – the Crab) at 8:10 p.m. AST
